worked_examples.final_answer: Largest impossible postage is 191 cents; 96/191 of integers from 1 to 191 are non-representable.
worked_examples.key_insight: Systematically checking all residues mod 13 (or mod 17) when verifying non-representability is exhaustive and complete; the fraction of gaps is always exactly (a-1)(b-1)/(2*(ab-a-b)).

common_pitfalls: Pitfall 1: Forgetting to verify gcd(a,b) = 1 before applying the formula; if gcd > 1, the formula gives a wrong answer and infinitely many values are non-representable.
Pitfall 2: Confusing the Frobenius number (largest NON-representable) with the smallest representable number greater than some threshold; always check whether the answer should be g(a,b) or g(a,b)+1.
Pitfall 3: Attempting to apply g(a,b) = ab - a - b to three or more denominations; no such simple closed form exists for three or more generators.

nodes.title: Generating Functions Algebraic Basics
nodes.definition: A generating function encodes a sequence {a_n} as coefficients of a formal power series G(x) = sum_{n>=0} a_n * x^n, enabling algebraic manipulation of sequences.
key_facts: Ordinary generating function (OGF): G(x) = sum_{n>=0} a_n * x^n; the coefficient [x^n] G(x) = a_n
Geometric series identity: sum_{n>=0} x^n = 1/(1-x) for |x| < 1, foundational for closed-form derivations
Scaling rule: if G(x) generates {a_n}, then G(c*x) generates {c^n * a_n}
Shift rule: if G(x) generates {a_n}, then (G(x) - a_0)/x generates {a_{n+1}}
Convolution rule: if F(x) generates {f_n} and G(x) generates {g_n}, then F(x)*G(x) generates {sum_{k=0}^{n} f_k * g_{n-k}}
Differentiation rule: x * G'(x) generates {n * a_n}, useful for extracting weighted sums

worked_examples.problem: Find the generating function for the sequence a_n = 3^n - 2^n for n >= 0, then extract a closed form for the coefficient of x^5.
solution_steps: Step 1: Write a_n = 3^n - 2^n, so G(x) = sum_{n>=0} (3^n - 2^n) x^n
Step 2: Split the sum: G(x) = sum_{n>=0} (3x)^n - sum_{n>=0} (2x)^n
Step 3: Apply geometric series formula to each: G(x) = 1/(1-3x) - 1/(1-2x)
Step 4: Combine over common denominator: G(x) = [(1-2x) - (1-3x)] / [(1-3x)(1-2x)] = x / [(1-3x)(1-2x)]
worked_examples.key_insight: Linearity of generating functions allows splitting sequences into simpler components, each handled by the geometric series formula independently.

worked_examples.problem: The sequence {b_n} satisfies b_0 = 1, b_n = b_{n-1} + 4 for n >= 1 (arithmetic sequence with common difference 4). Find the closed-form OGF and verify b_4.
solution_steps: Step 1: Identify b_n = 1 + 4n (arithmetic sequence starting at 1 with difference 4)
Step 2: Write G(x) = sum_{n>=0} (1 + 4n) x^n = sum_{n>=0} x^n + 4 * sum_{n>=0} n * x^n
Step 3: First sum: sum_{n>=0} x^n = 1/(1-x)
Step 4: For sum_{n>=0} n * x^n, use differentiation: d/dx [1/(1-x)] = 1/(1-x)^2, and x * d/dx [1/(1-x)] = x/(1-x)^2 generates {n * 1^n} = {n}
worked_examples.key_insight: The differentiation rule converts the generating function of {1} into the generating function of {n}, enabling compact OGFs for polynomial-indexed sequences.

worked_examples.problem: Use generating functions to count the number of ways to write n as an ordered sum of parts each from {1, 3, 5}. Find the count for n = 6.
solution_steps: Step 1: Each part chosen from {1,3,5} contributes a factor; since order matters (compositions), the OGF for a single part is x^1 + x^3 + x^5
Step 2: The OGF for any number of parts is G(x) = 1/(1 - (x + x^3 + x^5))
Step 3: Expand denominator: 1 - x - x^3 - x^5
Step 4: Compute coefficients up to x^6 by long division or recurrence: a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-3} + a_{n-5} with a_0=1, a_k=0 for k<0
Step 6: Verify a few: n=3 can be {3} or {1,1,1} or {1,1,1}... wait, ordered: (3), (1,1,1) = 2 ways. Correct.
worked_examples.final_answer: The number of ordered compositions of 6 using parts from {1,3,5} is 8
worked_examples.key_insight: The OGF for compositions is a geometric series in the single-part generating function; extracting coefficients via the induced recurrence avoids full polynomial expansion.

common_pitfalls: Pitfall 1: Confusing formal power series with convergent series — in combinatorics, x is a formal variable and convergence is irrelevant; applying radius-of-convergence reasoning incorrectly can cause errors.

Pitfall 2: Forgetting the shift when applying the recurrence-to-OGF conversion — multiplying G(x) by x shifts indices by 1, so summing from n=1 vs n=0 changes the boundary terms and must be handled separately.

Pitfall 3: Misapplying convolution — the product F(x)*G(x) gives the convolution sum_{k=0}^{n} f_k * g_{n-k}, not the pointwise product {f_n * g_n}; pointwise products require Hadamard product techniques instead.

nodes.title: Generating Functions for Counting
nodes.definition: A generating function encodes a sequence of counts as coefficients of a formal power series, transforming combinatorial counting problems into algebraic ones.
key_facts: Ordinary generating function (OGF): G(x) = sum_{n>=0} a_n * x^n, where a_n counts objects of size n
Product rule: if A(x) and B(x) are OGFs for independent choices, the combined OGF is A(x)*B(x), with [x^n] giving the convolution count
Geometric series identity: 1/(1-x)^k = sum_{n>=0} C(n+k-1, k-1) * x^n, key for stars-and-bars type problems
Exponential generating function (EGF): G(x) = sum_{n>=0} a_n * x^n / n!, used when order matters (labeled structures)
Extracting coefficients: [x^n] (1/(1-x)^k) = C(n+k-1, k-1); [x^n] (1+x)^m = C(m,n)

worked_examples.problem: In how many ways can you select a total of 11 items from 4 types, where type A has at most 3, type B has at most 4, type C has at most 5, and type D is unlimited?
solution_steps: Set up OGF: each type contributes a factor. Type A: (1 + x + x^2 + x^3), Type B: (1 + x + ... + x^4), Type C: (1 + x + ... + x^5), Type D: 1/(1-x)
Write each finite sum in closed form: (1-x^4)/(1-x) for A, (1-x^5)/(1-x) for B, (1-x^6)/(1-x) for C, 1/(1-x) for D
Expand using [x^n](1/(1-x)^4) = C(n+3,3), then subtract contributions from x^4, x^5, x^6 terms via inclusion-exclusion
Subtract triple: x^4*x^5*x^6=x^15 > x^11, so no contribution
worked_examples.key_insight: Finite upper bounds on each variable translate to finite polynomial factors in the OGF, and inclusion-exclusion on those factors handles the constraints cleanly.

worked_examples.problem: Find the number of ways to distribute 9 identical candies among 3 children so each child gets an odd number of candies.
solution_steps: Each child must receive an odd number: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, ... The OGF for one child is x + x^3 + x^5 + ... = x/(1-x^2)
For 3 children, the combined OGF is [x/(1-x^2)]^3 = x^3 / (1-x^2)^3
We need [x^9] in x^3/(1-x^2)^3, which equals [x^6] in 1/(1-x^2)^3
Substitute y = x^2: we need [y^3] in 1/(1-y)^3
worked_examples.key_insight: Restricting to odd values shifts and compresses the generating function via substitution, reducing the problem to a standard stars-and-bars coefficient extraction.

common_pitfalls: Pitfall 1: Confusing OGFs and EGFs - using EGF (dividing by n!) for unlabeled/unordered problems where OGF is appropriate, leading to off-by-factor errors.
Pitfall 2: Forgetting to apply inclusion-exclusion when upper bound constraints exist; simply using 1/(1-x)^k ignores the caps on each variable.
Pitfall 3: Incorrectly extracting coefficients after variable substitution, e.g., failing to account for the parity shift when replacing x^2 with y, confusing the index of extraction.

nodes.title: Geometric Probability via Measure Ratios
nodes.definition: Geometric probability assigns probabilities by comparing geometric measures (length, area, volume) of favorable outcomes to the total sample space measure.
key_facts: P(event) = measure(favorable region) / measure(total region), where measure is length, area, or volume
For a uniform distribution over a region S, P(point in A) = area(A) / area(S) for any subset A of S
Buffon's Needle: probability a needle of length L crosses a parallel line grid of spacing d (L <= d) is P = 2L / (pi * d)
For continuous uniform distributions, P(single point) = 0; only intervals/regions with positive measure have positive probability
Bertrand's paradox: geometric probability can be ambiguous when the sample space parameterization is not uniquely specified

worked_examples.problem: A point (x, y) is chosen uniformly at random inside a rectangle with vertices (0,0), (6,0), (6,4), (0,4). What is the probability that x^2 + y^2 < 9 (i.e., the point lies inside a circle of radius 3 centered at the origin)?
solution_steps: Step 1: Total area of rectangle = 6 * 4 = 24.
Step 2: The favorable region is the intersection of the disk x^2 + y^2 < 9 with the rectangle [0,6] x [0,4].
Step 3: The circle has radius 3 centered at origin. Within the rectangle (x >= 0, y >= 0), the circle arc goes from (3,0) to (0,3).
Step 4: The favorable region is a quarter-disk of radius 3 entirely contained in the rectangle (since 3 <= 4 and 3 <= 6).
Step 5: Area of quarter-disk = (1/4) * pi * 3^2 = 9*pi/4.
worked_examples.key_insight: Restrict the geometric region to the intersection of the favorable set and the sample space; verify the circular arc stays within the rectangle before assuming a clean quarter-disk.

worked_examples.problem: Two numbers a and b are chosen independently and uniformly at random from [0, 5]. What is the probability that |a - b| > 2?
solution_steps: Step 1: The sample space is the square [0,5] x [0,5] with total area = 25.
Step 2: The unfavorable region is |a - b| <= 2, i.e., -2 <= a - b <= 2, or equivalently the band between lines b = a - 2 and b = a + 2.
Step 3: It is easier to compute the favorable region directly: |a - b| > 2 means a - b > 2 or b - a > 2.
Step 4: Region where a - b > 2: triangle with vertices (2,0), (5,0), (5,3). Area = (1/2)*3*3 = 9/2.
Step 5: Region where b - a > 2: triangle with vertices (0,2), (0,5), (3,5). Area = (1/2)*3*3 = 9/2.
Step 6: Total favorable area = 9/2 + 9/2 = 9.
worked_examples.key_insight: Translating absolute value inequalities into two triangular regions in the 2D sample space is a classic geometric probability technique; symmetry about the diagonal confirms both triangles have equal area.

worked_examples.problem: A stick of length 10 is broken at two points chosen uniformly at random. What is the probability that the three pieces can form a triangle?
solution_steps: Step 1: Let the two break points be x and y chosen uniformly on [0,10]. WLOG represent them as (x,y) in the square [0,10] x [0,10], area = 100.
Step 2: The three piece lengths are min(x,y), |x-y|, and 10 - max(x,y). Normalize by dividing by 10: let u = x/10, v = y/10 in [0,1]^2.
Step 3: Triangle inequality requires each piece < 1/2 (of total length 10, each piece < 5).
Step 4: In the unit square, the three pieces (after sorting) satisfy the triangle inequality iff no piece >= 1/2.
Step 5: Favorable region is the unit square minus the three corner triangles where one piece >= 1/2.

Step 6: Each corner triangle has area 1/2 * (1/2)^2 ... actually: region where min(u,v) >= 1/2 has area (1/2)^2 = 1/4; region where |u-v| >= 1/2 has area 2*(1/2)*(1/2)/2 = 1/4; region where 1-max(u,v) >= 1/2 has area (1/2)^2 = 1/4.
Step 7: These three regions are disjoint, total unfavorable area = 3/4. Favorable area = 1 - 3/4 = 1/4.
Step 8: P = 1/4.
worked_examples.key_insight: The broken-stick triangle problem reduces to finding the area of a region defined by three simultaneous inequalities; the three 'bad' corner regions are disjoint and each has area 1/4 of the total, making inclusion-exclusion unnecessary.

common_pitfalls: Pitfall 1: Forgetting to intersect the favorable region with the actual sample space boundary, leading to over-counting area outside the defined region.
Pitfall 2: Assuming uniform distribution over length when the problem implies uniform over area (or vice versa), which changes the probability measure entirely.
Pitfall 3: Incorrectly computing the area of curved intersections (e.g., partial circles) by treating them as full sectors without checking whether the arc stays within the sample space.

nodes.title: Geometric Progressions and Series
nodes.definition: A geometric progression is a sequence where each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by a fixed constant ratio r, forming a core structure in algebra.
key_facts: nth term formula: a_n = a_1 * r^(n-1), where a_1 is the first term and r is the common ratio
Sum of first n terms: S_n = a_1 * (1 - r^n) / (1 - r) for r != 1; S_n = n * a_1 for r = 1
Sum of infinite geometric series: S_inf = a_1 / (1 - r), valid only when |r| < 1
Common ratio r = a_(n+1) / a_n for any consecutive pair of terms
Product of first n terms: P_n = (a_1 * a_n)^(n/2), using the symmetry of the sequence
If three numbers a, b, c are in GP then b^2 = a * c (geometric mean property)

worked_examples.problem: A sequence has first term 7 and common ratio 3. Find the 6th term and the sum of the first 6 terms.
solution_steps: Identify: a_1 = 7, r = 3, n = 6
Compute 3^6 = 729
worked_examples.key_insight: The sum formula requires careful sign handling when r > 1; factoring out negatives from numerator and denominator simplifies arithmetic.

worked_examples.problem: An infinite geometric series has first term 18 and sum 27. Find the common ratio and the 4th term.
solution_steps: Verify |r| = 1/3 < 1, so the infinite sum is valid
worked_examples.key_insight: Working backwards from the infinite sum formula to find r is a powerful technique; always verify |r| < 1 after solving.

worked_examples.problem: Three consecutive terms of a GP sum to 38 and their product is 1728. Find the three terms.
solution_steps: Let the three terms be a/r, a, a*r (symmetric form simplifies product)
Product: (a/r) * a * (a*r) = a^3 = 1728, so a = cube_root(1728) = 12
Sum: a/r + a + a*r = 38, substitute a = 12: 12/r + 12 + 12r = 38
Simplify: 12/r + 12r = 26, multiply by r: 12 + 12r^2 = 26r
Rearrange: 12r^2 - 26r + 12 = 0, divide by 2: 6r^2 - 13r + 6 = 0
For r = 3/2: terms are 8, 12, 18; for r = 2/3: terms are 18, 12, 8 (same set, reversed)
worked_examples.key_insight: Using a/r, a, a*r as the three terms makes the product collapse to a^3, immediately giving the middle term without needing to solve a system.

common_pitfalls: pitfall 1: Applying the infinite sum formula S_inf = a_1/(1-r) when |r| >= 1, where the series diverges and the formula is invalid.
pitfall 2: Confusing the index in the nth term formula; a_n = a_1 * r^(n-1) uses exponent n-1, not n, causing off-by-one errors.
pitfall 3: Assuming a sequence is geometric after checking only one pair of consecutive terms; always verify the ratio is constant across multiple pairs.

nodes.title: Geometry: Shapes, Space, and Measurement
nodes.definition: Geometry studies the properties, relationships, and measurements of points, lines, angles, surfaces, and solids in space.
key_facts: Pythagorean Theorem: a^2 + b^2 = c^2 for a right triangle with legs a, b and hypotenuse c
Sum of interior angles of a convex polygon with n sides: (n - 2) * 180 degrees
Area of a triangle: A = (1/2) * base * height = (1/2) * a * b * sin(C)
Circle: circumference C = 2*pi*r, area A = pi*r^2
Similar triangles: corresponding sides are proportional; if ratio is k, area ratio is k^2
Exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles

worked_examples.problem: A triangle has sides of length 7, 9, and 11. Find the cosine of the angle opposite the side of length 11, then compute the area of the triangle.
solution_steps: Label sides: a = 7, b = 9, c = 11, and C is the angle opposite c.
Apply the Law of Cosines: c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab*cos(C).
worked_examples.key_insight: The Law of Cosines generalizes the Pythagorean theorem to non-right triangles, and once an angle is known, the area formula A = (1/2)*a*b*sin(C) completes the computation efficiently.

worked_examples.problem: In a circle of radius 6, a chord PQ is drawn at a perpendicular distance of 4 from the center. A second chord RS passes through the midpoint M of PQ and is perpendicular to PQ. Find the lengths of PQ and RS.
solution_steps: Let O be the center and d = 4 be the perpendicular distance from O to chord PQ.
Half-length of PQ: using the right triangle formed, half-PQ = sqrt(r^2 - d^2) = sqrt(36 - 16) = sqrt(20) = 2*sqrt(5).
So PQ = 4*sqrt(5).
M is the midpoint of PQ, so OM = 4 (perpendicular distance).
RS passes through M and is perpendicular to PQ, meaning RS lies along the line OM extended.
The distance from O to chord RS: since RS is perpendicular to PQ and passes through M, RS lies along the diameter direction through M.
OM = 4, so M is at distance 4 from O along the diameter direction.

The chord RS is perpendicular to OM at M, so the perpendicular distance from O to RS equals OM = 4... but RS passes THROUGH M and is perpendicular to PQ (which is horizontal), so RS is vertical through M.

Distance from O to line RS = horizontal distance from O to M = 0 only if M is on the vertical through O. Re-examine: OM is perpendicular to PQ and has length 4, so RS passes through M along OM's direction (vertical). RS is the chord along the vertical line through M.

Distance from O to this vertical line = horizontal component = 0 if M is directly below O. Since OM ⊥ PQ and |OM| = 4, M lies on the perpendicular from O to PQ, so RS passes through M along OM, meaning RS is a diameter? No — RS passes through M perpendicular to PQ, which is the same direction as OM.
RS lies on the line through O and M (the perpendicular bisector of PQ), so RS is a diameter of the circle.
worked_examples.key_insight: The perpendicular from the center to a chord bisects it; a chord perpendicular to another chord at its midpoint must lie along the perpendicular bisector of that chord, which passes through the center, making it a diameter.

worked_examples.problem: A regular hexagon has a perimeter of 54. Find its area.
solution_steps: A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides, so side length s = 54/6 = 9.
A regular hexagon can be divided into 6 equilateral triangles, each with side length s = 9.
Area of one equilateral triangle with side s: A_tri = (sqrt(3)/4)*s^2 = (sqrt(3)/4)*81 = 81*sqrt(3)/4.
Total area of hexagon: A = 6 * (81*sqrt(3)/4) = 486*sqrt(3)/4 = 243*sqrt(3)/2.
worked_examples.key_insight: Decomposing a regular hexagon into 6 congruent equilateral triangles reduces the area calculation to a single triangle formula scaled by 6, exploiting the hexagon's rotational symmetry.

common_pitfalls: Angle mode confusion: using degrees instead of radians (or vice versa) in trigonometric area or length formulas, leading to incorrect results.
Forgetting that similar figures scale area by k^2 but perimeter by k — applying the same ratio to both area and length.
Assuming that a chord bisected by another chord implies perpendicularity; bisection and perpendicularity are independent properties unless additional conditions (like one being a diameter) are given.

nodes.title: Graph Theory Fundamentals and Combinatorics
nodes.definition: Graph theory studies structures of vertices connected by edges, providing combinatorial tools to count, color, and traverse networks.
key_facts: Handshaking Lemma: sum of all vertex degrees = 2|E|, so the number of odd-degree vertices is always even
Euler's formula for connected planar graphs: V - E + F = 2, where V = vertices, E = edges, F = faces
A connected graph has an Eulerian circuit iff every vertex has even degree; an Eulerian path exists iff exactly 2 vertices have odd degree
A tree on n vertices has exactly n - 1 edges and is the unique minimally connected graph on n vertices
The number of labeled trees on n vertices is n^(n-2) (Cayley's formula)
Complete graph K_n has C(n, 2) = n(n-1)/2 edges and is (n-1)-regular

worked_examples.problem: A connected graph has 9 vertices. Seven vertices have degree 4 and two vertices have degree 3. How many edges does the graph have, and verify the handshaking lemma holds?
solution_steps: Step 1: Sum all vertex degrees: 7 * 4 + 2 * 3 = 28 + 6 = 34.
Step 2: By the Handshaking Lemma, sum of degrees = 2|E|, so |E| = 34 / 2 = 17.
Step 3: Verify the count of odd-degree vertices: both degree-3 vertices are odd, giving exactly 2 odd-degree vertices, which is even — consistent with the lemma.
Step 4: Confirm: 17 edges in a connected graph on 9 vertices is plausible (a tree would need 8, so 17 edges means 17 - 8 = 9 extra edges creating cycles).
worked_examples.key_insight: The Handshaking Lemma converts degree information directly into edge counts; always verify the parity condition on odd-degree vertices as a consistency check.

worked_examples.problem: A connected planar graph has 11 vertices and 18 edges. How many faces does it have? Then verify that for a simple planar graph, E <= 3V - 6 holds.
solution_steps: Step 1: Apply Euler's formula: V - E + F = 2, so F = 2 - V + E = 2 - 11 + 18 = 9.
Step 2: The graph has 9 faces (including the outer/unbounded face).
Step 3: Check the inequality E <= 3V - 6: 3V - 6 = 3(11) - 6 = 33 - 6 = 27.
Step 4: Since E = 18 <= 27, the inequality holds, confirming planarity is not contradicted.
Step 5: Note the bound E <= 3V - 6 comes from each face being bounded by at least 3 edges and each edge bordering at most 2 faces: 2E >= 3F, combined with Euler's formula.
worked_examples.key_insight: Euler's formula V - E + F = 2 is a powerful invariant: knowing any two of {V, E, F} determines the third, and it also yields planarity bounds by combining with face-edge incidence counting.

worked_examples.problem: How many labeled trees can be formed on 6 vertices? List the degree sequence of one such tree where one vertex has degree 4.
solution_steps: Step 1: By Cayley's formula, the number of labeled trees on n vertices is n^(n-2).
Step 2: For n = 6: 6^(6-2) = 6^4 = 1296 labeled trees.
Step 3: For a tree on 6 vertices with one vertex of degree 4: the tree has n - 1 = 5 edges.
Step 4: By the Handshaking Lemma, sum of degrees = 2 * 5 = 10.
Step 5: If one vertex has degree 4, the remaining 5 vertices must have degrees summing to 10 - 4 = 6, with each degree >= 1 (since the tree is connected).
Step 6: A valid degree sequence: (4, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1) — one hub of degree 4, one vertex of degree 2, and four leaves. Sum = 4+2+1+1+1+1 = 10. Confirmed.
worked_examples.final_answer: 1296 labeled trees on 6 vertices; example degree sequence (4, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1).
worked_examples.key_insight: Cayley's formula n^(n-2) counts labeled trees exponentially, and degree sequences in trees are tightly constrained by the fixed edge count n-1 and the Handshaking Lemma.

common_pitfalls: Pitfall 1: Confusing Eulerian circuits (visit every EDGE once) with Hamiltonian cycles (visit every VERTEX once) — the degree-parity condition applies only to Eulerian circuits.
Pitfall 2: Forgetting to count the outer (unbounded) face when applying Euler's formula V - E + F = 2 to planar graphs, leading to F being off by 1.
Pitfall 3: Assuming a graph with n vertices and n-1 edges is always a tree — it must also be connected; a disconnected graph can have n-1 edges without being a tree.

nodes.title: Greatest Common Divisor and LCM
nodes.definition: In number theory, the GCD of two integers is the largest positive integer dividing both, while the LCM is the smallest positive integer divisible by both.
key_facts: Fundamental relationship: gcd(a, b) * lcm(a, b) = a * b for positive integers a, b
Prime factorization rule: gcd(a, b) uses min of each prime's exponent; lcm(a, b) uses max of each prime's exponent
Euclidean algorithm: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), terminating when remainder is 0
Bezout's identity: there exist integers x, y such that gcd(a, b) = a*x + b*y
For three integers: lcm(a, b, c) = lcm(lcm(a, b), c); gcd(a, b, c) = gcd(gcd(a, b), c)
gcd(a, b) = gcd(a, b - a) = gcd(a, b mod a), showing gcd is invariant under subtraction

worked_examples.problem: Find gcd(2457, 1638) using the Euclidean algorithm, then compute lcm(2457, 1638).
solution_steps: Apply Euclidean algorithm: 2457 = 1 * 1638 + 819
Since remainder is 0, gcd(2457, 1638) = 819
Use fundamental relationship: lcm(2457, 1638) = (2457 * 1638) / gcd(2457, 1638)
worked_examples.key_insight: When one number is an exact multiple of the other (2457 = 3 * 819, 1638 = 2 * 819), the Euclidean algorithm terminates in very few steps, and lcm equals their product divided by gcd.

worked_examples.problem: Three bells ring at intervals of 36, 54, and 90 seconds respectively. If they all ring together at time 0, after how many seconds do they next all ring simultaneously? Also find the largest time interval that divides all three periods.
solution_steps: Compute lcm by taking max exponent of each prime: lcm = 2^2 * 3^3 * 5^1 = 4 * 27 * 5 = 540
Compute gcd by taking min exponent of each prime: gcd = 2^1 * 3^2 * 5^0 = 2 * 9 = 18
Verify: 540/36 = 15, 540/54 = 10, 540/90 = 6 — all integers, confirming lcm = 540
Verify: 36/18 = 2, 54/18 = 3, 90/18 = 5 — all integers, confirming gcd = 18
worked_examples.final_answer: They next ring together after 540 seconds; the largest common divisor of all three periods is 18 seconds.
worked_examples.key_insight: For three or more numbers, use prime factorization directly: lcm takes max exponents and gcd takes min exponents across all numbers simultaneously, which is more efficient than repeated pairwise computation.

worked_examples.problem: Find all pairs of positive integers (a, b) with a <= b such that gcd(a, b) = 14 and lcm(a, b) = 1260.
solution_steps: Write a = 14m and b = 14n where gcd(m, n) = 1 (m, n are coprime)
Then lcm(a, b) = 14mn = 1260, so mn = 90
Find all pairs (m, n) with m <= n, mn = 90, and gcd(m, n) = 1
worked_examples.key_insight: When gcd and lcm are both specified, write a = gcd*m and b = gcd*n with gcd(m,n)=1; then mn = lcm/gcd, reducing the problem to finding coprime factor pairs of a smaller number.

common_pitfalls: Pitfall: Applying gcd(a,b)*lcm(a,b)=a*b to three or more numbers — this identity holds ONLY for exactly two numbers; for three numbers, lcm(a,b,c)*gcd(a,b,c) does NOT generally equal a*b*c.
Pitfall: Confusing min/max in prime factorization — gcd uses the MINIMUM exponent and lcm uses the MAXIMUM; reversing these gives the wrong answer.
Pitfall: Forgetting that lcm and gcd require positive integers; applying the Euclidean algorithm carelessly to negative numbers or zero without adjusting can produce incorrect results.

nodes.title: Half Angle Trigonometric Formulas
nodes.definition: Half-angle formulas express trig functions of θ/2 in terms of trig functions of θ, derived from double-angle identities by substitution.
key_facts: sin(θ/2) = ±sqrt((1 - cos θ) / 2), sign depends on quadrant of θ/2
cos(θ/2) = ±sqrt((1 + cos θ) / 2), sign depends on quadrant of θ/2
tan(θ/2) = ±sqrt((1 - cos θ) / (1 + cos θ)) = sin θ / (1 + cos θ) = (1 - cos θ) / sin θ
The tan(θ/2) forms without square roots are unambiguous in sign: tan(θ/2) = sin θ / (1 + cos θ)
Half-angle formulas are derived by solving cos θ = 1 - 2sin²(θ/2) and cos θ = 2cos²(θ/2) - 1 for the half-angle

worked_examples.problem: Given that cos(θ) = -7/25 and θ is in the second quadrant, find the exact value of sin(θ/2) and cos(θ/2).
solution_steps: Step 1: Determine the quadrant of θ/2. Since θ is in Q2, we have 90° < θ < 180°, so 45° < θ/2 < 90°, meaning θ/2 is in Q1. Both sin(θ/2) and cos(θ/2) are positive.
Step 3: Compute numerator: 1 + 7/25 = 32/25, so (32/25) / 2 = 16/25
Step 4: sin(θ/2) = sqrt(16/25) = 4/5
worked_examples.key_insight: Determining the quadrant of θ/2 from the quadrant of θ resolves the ± ambiguity in the square-root form of the half-angle formulas.

worked_examples.problem: Use the half-angle formula to find the exact value of tan(112.5°).
solution_steps: Step 1: Recognize 112.5° = 225°/2, so we need tan(225°/2) with θ = 225°.
Step 2: Use the sign-unambiguous form: tan(θ/2) = (1 - cos θ) / sin θ
Step 3: Compute cos(225°) = -sqrt(2)/2 and sin(225°) = -sqrt(2)/2
Step 5: Simplify numerator: (2 + sqrt(2)) / 2; denominator: -sqrt(2)/2
Step 6: Divide: [(2 + sqrt(2))/2] / [-sqrt(2)/2] = (2 + sqrt(2)) / (-sqrt(2))
Step 7: Rationalize: (2 + sqrt(2)) / (-sqrt(2)) * (sqrt(2)/sqrt(2)) = (2sqrt(2) + 2) / (-2) = -(sqrt(2) + 1)
Step 8: Verify sign: 112.5° is in Q2, so tan is negative. -(sqrt(2)+1) < 0 ✓
worked_examples.key_insight: The quotient forms of tan(θ/2) avoid the ± sign issue entirely, making them preferable when the half-angle lies in Q2 or Q3 where sign determination could be error-prone.

worked_examples.problem: Simplify the expression sqrt((1 - cos(4α)) / (1 + cos(4α))) assuming 0 < α < π/4.
solution_steps: Step 1: Recognize the structure matches tan²(θ/2) = (1 - cos θ) / (1 + cos θ) with θ = 4α.
Step 2: So the expression equals sqrt(tan²(2α)) = |tan(2α)|.
Step 3: Determine the sign of tan(2α): since 0 < α < π/4, we have 0 < 2α < π/2, so tan(2α) > 0.
Step 4: Therefore |tan(2α)| = tan(2α).
worked_examples.key_insight: Recognizing the half-angle structure inside a square root allows collapsing the expression to a single trig function; the domain constraint is essential to resolve the absolute value.

common_pitfalls: Pitfall 1: Forgetting the ± sign in the square-root forms — the sign must be chosen based on the quadrant of θ/2, not θ itself.
Pitfall 2: Using the wrong θ — the formula for sin(θ/2) uses cos(θ), not cos(θ/2); students sometimes substitute the half-angle value into both sides.
Pitfall 3: Overlooking the sign-unambiguous tan(θ/2) alternatives; using the square-root form unnecessarily introduces sign errors when sin θ or (1 - cos θ)/sin θ forms are cleaner.

nodes.title: Heron's Formula Triangle Area
nodes.definition: Heron's formula computes the area of a triangle solely from its three side lengths using the semi-perimeter, without requiring knowledge of any angle.
key_facts: For a triangle with sides a, b, c: Area = sqrt(s*(s-a)*(s-b)*(s-c)), where s = (a+b+c)/2
Semi-perimeter: s = (a+b+c)/2; each factor (s-a), (s-b), (s-c) is strictly positive for a valid triangle
Equivalent form: Area = (1/4)*sqrt((a+b+c)(-a+b+c)(a-b+c)(a+b-c))
Degenerate case: if s*(s-a)*(s-b)*(s-c) = 0, the triangle has zero area (collinear points)
Heron's formula is equivalent to Area = (1/2)*a*b*sin(C) via the law of cosines substitution
For an equilateral triangle with side a: Area = (sqrt(3)/4)*a^2, recoverable from Heron's formula

worked_examples.problem: Find the area of a triangle with sides a=13, b=14, c=15.
solution_steps: Compute semi-perimeter: s = (13+14+15)/2 = 42/2 = 21
Compute (s-a) = 21-13 = 8
Compute (s-b) = 21-14 = 7
Compute (s-c) = 21-15 = 6
Take square root: Area = sqrt(7056) = 84
worked_examples.key_insight: Choosing sides that yield a perfect square under the radical avoids irrational answers; recognizing 21*8*7*6 = 7056 = 84^2 is the key computational step.

worked_examples.problem: A triangle has sides of length 7, 9, and 11. Find its area to three decimal places.
solution_steps: Compute semi-perimeter: s = (7+9+11)/2 = 27/2 = 13.5
worked_examples.key_insight: When sides are odd integers, the semi-perimeter is a half-integer, so each factor (s-a) etc. is also a half-integer; the product of four half-integers can still yield a manageable decimal.

worked_examples.problem: Verify that a triangle with sides 5, 12, and 13 is a right triangle using Heron's formula, then confirm with the standard formula.
solution_steps: Compute semi-perimeter: s = (5+12+13)/2 = 30/2 = 15
Area = sqrt(900) = 30
Verify with right-triangle formula: Area = (1/2)*leg1*leg2 = (1/2)*5*12 = 30
Both methods agree, confirming the triangle is right-angled (hypotenuse 13)
worked_examples.key_insight: Using Heron's formula as a cross-check against the base-height formula for a Pythagorean triple demonstrates consistency and can serve as a verification strategy.

common_pitfalls: Pitfall 1: Forgetting to halve the perimeter — using s = a+b+c instead of s = (a+b+c)/2 leads to a wildly incorrect area.
Pitfall 2: Not verifying the triangle inequality first; if any factor (s-a), (s-b), or (s-c) is negative or zero, the inputs do not form a valid non-degenerate triangle.
Pitfall 3: Rounding the semi-perimeter prematurely when sides are not integers, which compounds error inside the square root.

nodes.title: Hockey Stick Identity in Combinatorics
nodes.definition: The hockey stick identity states that summing consecutive binomial coefficients along a diagonal of Pascal's triangle yields a single binomial coefficient one row lower and one column over.
key_facts: fact 1: Sum form: C(r,r) + C(r+1,r) + C(r+2,r) + ... + C(n,r) = C(n+1, r+1)
fact 2: Equivalent left-side form: sum_{i=r}^{n} C(i, r) = C(n+1, r+1)
fact 3: Special case r=1: 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = C(n+1, 2) = n(n+1)/2, recovering the triangular number formula
fact 4: Special case r=0: summing n+1 ones gives C(n+1,1) = n+1, confirming the base case
fact 5: Proof via Pascal's identity: C(n+1,r+1) = C(n,r) + C(n,r+1), applied recursively collapses the sum
fact 6: Combinatorial proof: choosing r+1 items from {1,...,n+1} where the largest chosen element determines which term in the sum is selected

worked_examples.problem: Compute C(3,3) + C(4,3) + C(5,3) + C(6,3) + C(7,3) + C(8,3) without expanding each term individually.
solution_steps: Identify the pattern: each term has bottom index r=3, and top index runs from i=3 to i=8.
Apply the hockey stick identity: sum_{i=3}^{8} C(i,3) = C(9, 4).
worked_examples.key_insight: Recognizing that all terms share the same bottom index r=3 allows immediate application of the hockey stick identity, collapsing a 6-term sum into a single binomial coefficient.

worked_examples.problem: How many ways can you choose 4 numbers from {1, 2, 3, ..., 13} such that the smallest chosen number is at least 2? Express the answer using the hockey stick identity.
solution_steps: We need to count 4-element subsets of {2, 3, ..., 13}, which has 12 elements.
This equals C(12, 4) = 495 directly, but let us also derive it via hockey stick to illustrate the identity.
Condition on the value of the smallest element m, where m ranges from 2 to 10 (since we need 4 elements and the largest is 13).
If smallest element is m, the remaining 3 elements are chosen from {m+1, ..., 13}, giving C(13-m, 3) ways.
Reindex: let j = 13-m, so j runs from 3 to 11: sum_{j=3}^{11} C(j, 3).
Apply hockey stick: sum_{j=3}^{11} C(j,3) = C(12, 4).
worked_examples.key_insight: Conditioning on the minimum element of a subset naturally produces a sum of binomial coefficients with the same lower index, which the hockey stick identity collapses into a single term. This double-counting argument proves the identity combinatorially.

worked_examples.problem: Find the value of sum_{k=2}^{9} C(k, 2) * 1 (i.e., C(2,2)+C(3,2)+...+C(9,2)) and use it to compute 1+3+6+10+15+21+28+36.
solution_steps: Recognize that C(k,2) = k(k-1)/2 gives the k-th triangular number (offset): C(2,2)=1, C(3,2)=3, C(4,2)=6, C(5,2)=10, C(6,2)=15, C(7,2)=21, C(8,2)=28, C(9,2)=36.
Apply hockey stick with r=2, summing from i=2 to i=9: sum_{i=2}^{9} C(i,2) = C(10, 3).
worked_examples.key_insight: Triangular numbers are themselves binomial coefficients C(k,2), so summing them is exactly a hockey stick sum. This shows the identity unifies sums of triangular numbers, just as the r=1 case unifies sums of integers.

common_pitfalls: pitfall 1: Off-by-one in the result — the identity gives C(n+1, r+1), not C(n, r+1) or C(n+1, r). Always increment both the top index by 1 and the bottom index by 1 relative to the largest term in the sum.

pitfall 2: Forgetting the starting index must equal r — the sum must begin at C(r, r)=1. If the sum starts at C(m, r) with m > r, you must subtract the missing initial terms: sum_{i=m}^{n} C(i,r) = C(n+1,r+1) - C(m,r+1).

pitfall 3: Confusing which index is fixed — the bottom index r must be constant across all terms. If the top index is fixed and the bottom index varies, a different identity (Vandermonde's) applies instead.

nodes.title: Hypergeometric Distribution Sampling Without Replacement
nodes.definition: Models the probability of k successes drawn from a finite population of N items containing K successes, when sampling n items without replacement.
key_facts: PMF: P(X = k) = C(K, k) * C(N-K, n-k) / C(N, n), for max(0, n+K-N) <= k <= min(n, K)
Mean: E[X] = n * K / N
Variance: Var(X) = n * (K/N) * ((N-K)/N) * (N-n)/(N-1)
The factor (N-n)/(N-1) is the finite population correction factor, distinguishing it from binomial variance
Sum identity: sum over k of C(K,k)*C(N-K,n-k) = C(N,n), reflecting Vandermonde's identity
As N -> infinity with K/N -> p fixed, the hypergeometric distribution converges to Binomial(n, p)

worked_examples.problem: A box contains 18 light bulbs, of which 7 are defective. An inspector randomly selects 6 bulbs without replacement. What is the probability that exactly 2 of the selected bulbs are defective?
solution_steps: Identify parameters: N=18 (total), K=7 (defective), n=6 (drawn), k=2 (desired defectives)
worked_examples.key_insight: The numerator counts favorable arrangements by separately choosing defectives from defective pool and non-defectives from non-defective pool, then dividing by all ways to choose n from N.

worked_examples.problem: A committee of 5 is chosen from 9 economists and 6 sociologists. Find the expected number of sociologists on the committee and the probability the committee has at most 1 sociologist.
solution_steps: Identify parameters: N=15, K=6 (sociologists), n=5, X = number of sociologists
Expected value: E[X] = n*K/N = 5*6/15 = 2
For P(X <= 1), compute P(X=0) + P(X=1)
worked_examples.key_insight: Expected value has a clean closed form n*K/N regardless of distribution shape; computing tail probabilities requires summing individual PMF terms.

worked_examples.problem: From a deck of 52 cards, 8 cards are dealt. What is the variance in the number of hearts received, and what is the finite population correction factor here?
solution_steps: Identify: N=52, K=13 (hearts), n=8
Variance formula: Var(X) = n*(K/N)*((N-K)/N)*(N-n)/(N-1)
Finite population correction: (N-n)/(N-1) = (52-8)/(52-1) = 44/51
Compare to binomial variance without correction: 8*(1/4)*(3/4) = 3/2 = 1.5, vs 22/17 ≈ 1.294
worked_examples.key_insight: Sampling without replacement reduces variance compared to binomial because drawing one item changes the composition of the remaining pool, creating negative correlation between draws.

common_pitfalls: Pitfall 1: Confusing hypergeometric with binomial — binomial assumes replacement (constant p per draw), hypergeometric does not; using binomial formula when sampling without replacement from a small population gives wrong probabilities.
Pitfall 2: Forgetting the valid range of k — k must satisfy both k <= K (can't draw more successes than exist) and n-k <= N-K (can't draw more failures than exist), so k >= max(0, n+K-N).
Pitfall 3: Omitting the finite population correction factor when computing variance, leading to overestimation of spread, especially when n is a large fraction of N.

nodes.title: Incenter Excenter Lemma Circle Properties
nodes.definition: The incenter-excenter lemma states that if I is the incenter of triangle ABC, then the circumcenter of triangle BIC lies on the circumcircle of ABC, and specific midpoint-circle relationships hold.
key_facts: fact 1: If M_A is the midpoint of arc BC not containing A, then M_A is the circumcenter of triangle BIC, meaning M_A B = M_A I = M_A C
fact 2: The excenters I_A, I_B, I_C of triangle ABC all lie on the circumcircle of triangle formed by arc midpoints M_A, M_B, M_C
fact 3: angle BIC = 90 + A/2, where A is the angle at vertex A of triangle ABC
fact 4: The midpoint of segment I*I_A (where I_A is the A-excenter) lies on the circumcircle of triangle ABC
fact 5: M_A is equidistant from B, I, C, and I_A, so M_A lies on the perpendicular bisector of both BC and II_A

worked_examples.problem: In triangle PQR with angles P=50, Q=70, R=60 degrees, let I be the incenter. Find angle QIR and verify that the midpoint M of arc QR (not containing P) satisfies M*Q = M*I.
solution_steps: Step 1: Use the formula angle QIR = 90 + P/2 = 90 + 50/2 = 90 + 25 = 115 degrees.
Step 2: The midpoint M of arc QR not containing P subtends arc QM = arc MR, so arc QR (not containing P) = 360 - 2*50 = 260... wait, arc QR not containing P = 2*angle QPR = 2*50 = 100 degrees.
Step 3: So arc QM = arc MR = 50 degrees each.
Step 4: By the incenter-excenter lemma, M is the circumcenter of triangle QIR, so MQ = MI = MR.

Step 5: To confirm MQ = MI: angle MQI = angle MQR + angle RQI. angle MQR = (arc MR)/2 = 25 degrees (inscribed angle). angle RQI = Q/2 = 35 degrees. So angle MQI = 60 degrees. Similarly angle MIQ = 60 degrees (since triangle MQI is isoceles with MQ=MI). This confirms MQ = MI.
Step 6: Therefore angle QIR = 115 degrees and MQ = MI = MR is verified.
worked_examples.final_answer: angle QIR = 115 degrees; M is equidistant from Q, I, and R
worked_examples.key_insight: The arc midpoint M of arc BC acts as the circumcenter of triangle BIC, a non-obvious fact that follows from angle chasing with the inscribed angle theorem.

worked_examples.problem: Triangle XYZ has circumradius R = 13. The incenter is I and the X-excenter is I_X. If angle X = 80 degrees, find the distance from the midpoint N of segment II_X to the circumcenter O, and show N lies on the circumcircle.
solution_steps: Step 1: By the incenter-excenter lemma, the midpoint N of segment II_X lies on the circumcircle of triangle XYZ.
Step 2: Specifically, N is the midpoint of arc YZ not containing X.
Step 3: Since N lies on the circumcircle of radius R = 13, the distance from O to N equals R = 13.
Step 4: To verify N is the arc midpoint: arc YZ not containing X = 2 * angle X = 2 * 80 = 160 degrees.
Step 5: N bisects this arc, so arc YN = arc NZ = 80 degrees each.
Step 6: The key property is that NI = NY = NZ (N is circumcenter of triangle YIZ), and since I and I_X are reflections over N in a specific sense, N is the midpoint of II_X.
Step 7: Therefore ON = R = 13, confirming N lies on the circumcircle.
worked_examples.final_answer: The distance from O to N equals R = 13; N lies on the circumcircle
worked_examples.key_insight: The midpoint of the segment connecting the incenter to an excenter always lies on the circumcircle, specifically at the arc midpoint opposite that excenter's vertex.

common_pitfalls: pitfall 1: Confusing which arc midpoint corresponds to which excenter; M_A (midpoint of arc BC not containing A) is the circumcenter of triangle BIC and also the midpoint of segment II_A.
pitfall 2: Forgetting that angle BIC = 90 + A/2, not 90 - A/2; the incenter creates an obtuse angle at I when A is acute.
pitfall 3: Assuming the result only applies to acute triangles; the incenter-excenter lemma holds for all triangle types.

nodes.title: Inclusion-Exclusion Principle
nodes.definition: A combinatorial technique that computes the size of a union of sets by alternately adding and subtracting the sizes of all intersections, correcting for overcounting.
key_facts: Two sets: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B|
Three sets: |A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A| + |B| + |C| - |A ∩ B| - |A ∩ C| - |B ∩ C| + |A ∩ B ∩ C|
General formula: |A_1 ∪ ... ∪ A_n| = sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^(k+1) * sum_{|S|=k} |intersection of sets in S|
Complementary form: elements in NONE of n sets = |Universe| - |A_1 ∪ ... ∪ A_n|, useful for counting restricted arrangements
Connection to derangements: D(n) = n! * sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k / k!, derived directly via inclusion-exclusion on forbidden fixed points
Surjection count: number of surjections from n elements to k elements = sum_{j=0}^{k} (-1)^j * C(k,j) * (k-j)^n

worked_examples.problem: Among integers from 1 to 300, how many are divisible by 4, 6, or 10?
solution_steps: Define A = multiples of 4 in [1,300], B = multiples of 6, C = multiples of 10
Apply inclusion-exclusion: 75 + 50 + 30 - 25 - 15 - 10 + 5 = 110
worked_examples.key_insight: When sets are defined by divisibility, intersections correspond to LCMs, making inclusion-exclusion straightforward to apply systematically.

worked_examples.problem: In how many ways can 7 distinct books be arranged on a shelf so that none of the 3 specific books (B1, B2, B3) occupies its own designated position (position 1, 2, 3 respectively), while books B4-B7 may go anywhere?
solution_steps: Total arrangements = 7!
Let A_i = arrangements where book B_i is in its forbidden position, for i = 1, 2, 3
|A_1| = 6! (fix B1 in pos 1, arrange remaining 6 freely)
|A_2| = 6!, |A_3| = 6! by symmetry
|A_1 ∩ A_2| = 5! (fix both B1 and B2 in their positions)
Valid arrangements = 7! - 1824 = 5040 - 1824 = 3216
worked_examples.key_insight: This is a partial derangement problem; only a subset of positions have restrictions, so inclusion-exclusion subtracts exactly the bad cases without over-restricting the unconstrained elements.

worked_examples.problem: How many 5-digit strings over {1,2,3,4} use every digit at least once? (Note: only 4 digits, 5 positions, so exactly one digit repeats.)
solution_steps: We count surjections from a 5-element set (positions) onto a 4-element set (digits)
Total functions (no restriction): 4^5 = 1024
Let A_i = strings missing digit i, for i = 1,2,3,4
|A_i| = 3^5 = 243 each (only 3 digits available)
|A_i ∩ A_j| = 2^5 = 32 each (only 2 digits available)
|A_i ∩ A_j ∩ A_k| = 1^5 = 1 each (only 1 digit)
|A_1 ∩ A_2 ∩ A_3 ∩ A_4| = 0 (no digits left)
Surjections = 1024 - 784 = 240
worked_examples.key_insight: Counting surjections via inclusion-exclusion on 'missing element' sets is a canonical application; the alternating sum corrects for strings missing multiple digits simultaneously.

common_pitfalls: Pitfall 1: Forgetting to alternate signs correctly — intersections of even cardinality are subtracted, odd cardinality are added; reversing this leads to wrong answers.
Pitfall 2: Miscalculating intersections by using GCD instead of LCM for divisibility problems — intersections of divisibility sets require LCM, not GCD.
Pitfall 3: Applying inclusion-exclusion to count elements satisfying ALL conditions rather than AT LEAST ONE, confusing union with intersection logic.

nodes.title: Independence of Events in Probability
nodes.definition: Two events A and B are independent if knowing one occurred gives no information about the other, formally P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B).
key_facts: Independence condition: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B)
Equivalent characterization: P(A | B) = P(A) whenever P(B) > 0
Mutual independence of n events requires P(A_i1 ∩ ... ∩ A_ik) = P(A_i1)*...*P(A_ik) for ALL subsets, not just pairs
If A and B are independent, then so are A and B^c, A^c and B, and A^c and B^c
Disjoint events with positive probability are NEVER independent: P(A ∩ B) = 0 ≠ P(A)*P(B) > 0
For independent events: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A)*P(B)

worked_examples.problem: A biased coin has P(Heads) = 0.4. You flip it 3 times independently. What is the probability that you get Heads on the first flip AND Tails on the third flip, but NOT necessarily on the second?
solution_steps: Define events: A = Heads on flip 1, B = Tails on flip 3. The second flip is unrestricted.
Since flips are independent, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B).
P(A) = 0.4 (probability of Heads on flip 1).
P(B) = P(Tails on flip 3) = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6.
The second flip does not affect the calculation since we impose no condition on it.
worked_examples.key_insight: When events concern different independent trials, the multiplication rule applies directly regardless of other unrestricted trials in the sequence.

worked_examples.problem: A factory has two machines, X and Y. Machine X fails on any given day with probability 0.05, and machine Y fails independently with probability 0.08. What is the probability that on a given day at least one machine is working?
solution_steps: Let F_X = event X fails, F_Y = event Y fails. These are independent.
We want P(at least one machine working) = 1 - P(both machines fail).
P(both fail) = P(F_X ∩ F_Y) = P(F_X) * P(F_Y) by independence.
P(at least one working) = 1 - 0.004 = 0.996.
worked_examples.key_insight: Using complementary counting with independence: P(both fail) factors into a product, making the complement approach clean and efficient.

worked_examples.problem: Three students A, B, C each independently solve a puzzle with probabilities 2/5, 1/3, and 3/7 respectively. Verify whether pairwise independence alone guarantees the three events are mutually independent by checking the triple intersection.
solution_steps: Let events be A (student A solves), B (student B solves), C (student C solves).
For mutual independence, we need P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = P(A)*P(B)*P(C).
Since the problem states they solve independently, P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = 2/35 as well.
All pairwise products also check out: P(A∩B) = 2/15, P(A∩C) = 6/35, P(B∩C) = 3/21 = 1/7.
Mutual independence holds here because the problem explicitly states independence, but note: pairwise independence does NOT in general imply mutual independence.
worked_examples.final_answer: P(all three solve) = 2/35; mutual independence holds given the stated conditions, but pairwise independence alone is insufficient in general.
worked_examples.key_insight: Mutual independence is strictly stronger than pairwise independence; one must verify the product rule holds for ALL subsets of events, not just pairs.

common_pitfalls: Pitfall 1: Confusing mutually exclusive (disjoint) events with independent events — disjoint events with positive probability are actually maximally dependent, not independent.
Pitfall 2: Assuming pairwise independence implies mutual independence — three events can be pairwise independent yet fail P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = P(A)*P(B)*P(C).
Pitfall 3: Applying the multiplication rule P(A ∩ B) = P(A)*P(B) without verifying independence — this formula only holds when events are truly independent.

nodes.title: Indicator Random Variables in Probability
nodes.definition: An indicator random variable I_A takes value 1 if event A occurs and 0 otherwise, encoding membership in an event as a Bernoulli random variable.
key_facts: Definition: I_A = 1 if event A occurs, I_A = 0 otherwise
Expected value: E[I_A] = P(A), since E[I_A] = 1*P(A) + 0*P(A^c) = P(A)
Product rule: I_{A ∩ B} = I_A * I_B, so events A and B both occur iff their indicators multiply to 1
Union formula: I_{A ∪ B} = I_A + I_B - I_A * I_B
Variance: Var(I_A) = P(A)*(1 - P(A)) = P(A)*P(A^c)
Sum decomposition: for a count X = number of events among A_1,...,A_n that occur, X = I_{A_1} + ... + I_{A_n}, so E[X] = sum of P(A_i) by linearity

worked_examples.problem: A bag contains 6 red and 4 blue marbles. You draw 3 marbles without replacement. Let X be the number of red marbles drawn. Find E[X] using indicator random variables.
solution_steps: Define I_j = 1 if the j-th marble drawn is red, for j = 1, 2, 3.
Then X = I_1 + I_2 + I_3.
By linearity of expectation, E[X] = E[I_1] + E[I_2] + E[I_3].
By symmetry of sampling without replacement, P(j-th draw is red) = 6/10 for each j.
So E[I_j] = 6/10 = 3/5 for each j.
Therefore E[X] = 3 * (3/5) = 9/5.
worked_examples.key_insight: Indicator variables sidestep the hypergeometric distribution computation entirely. By symmetry, each draw position has the same marginal probability of being red, making the expectation trivial via linearity.

worked_examples.problem: Seven people sit randomly at a round table with 7 fixed seats. Let X be the number of people who sit directly to the right of a person taller than themselves. Find E[X].
solution_steps: Label the 7 seats 1 through 7 arranged in a circle. For each person i, define I_i = 1 if person i sits directly to the right of someone taller.
By linearity of expectation, E[X] = sum of E[I_i] = 7 * P(a given person has a taller neighbor immediately to their left).
Consider any fixed person p and their left neighbor q. Since all 7! arrangements are equally likely, p and q are equally likely to be in any relative order.
P(q is taller than p) = 1/2 by symmetry of the random arrangement.
So E[I_i] = 1/2 for each i.
Therefore E[X] = 7 * (1/2) = 7/2.
worked_examples.key_insight: Indicator variables reduce a complex circular arrangement problem to a single pairwise comparison. Symmetry ensures each adjacent pair is equally likely to be in either order, regardless of the global arrangement.

worked_examples.problem: A fair 8-sided die (faces 1–8) is rolled 5 times independently. Let X be the number of rolls that show a prime number (2, 3, 5, 7). Find E[X] and Var(X).
solution_steps: The primes on an 8-sided die are {2, 3, 5, 7}, so P(prime on one roll) = 4/8 = 1/2.
Define I_j = 1 if roll j shows a prime, for j = 1, ..., 5.
Since rolls are independent, Var(X) = sum of Var(I_j).
Var(I_j) = P(prime) * P(not prime) = (1/2)*(1/2) = 1/4.
Therefore Var(X) = 5 * (1/4) = 5/4.
worked_examples.key_insight: When indicator variables are independent (as with independent trials), variance also decomposes additively. This is a direct route to the binomial distribution's mean and variance formulas.

common_pitfalls: Pitfall 1: Confusing E[I_A] = P(A) with E[I_A^2] = P(A); both are equal since I_A^2 = I_A, but students sometimes misapply this when computing variance, forgetting Var(I_A) = E[I_A^2] - (E[I_A])^2 = P(A) - P(A)^2.

Pitfall 2: Assuming indicators for dependent events have independent variances. When I_{A_i} are not independent (e.g., sampling without replacement), Var(sum of I_i) requires adding covariance terms: Var(X) = sum Var(I_i) + 2*sum_{i<j} Cov(I_i, I_j).
Pitfall 3: Incorrectly writing I_{A ∪ B} = I_A + I_B without subtracting I_A * I_B, leading to overcounting when both events occur simultaneously.

nodes.title: AM-GM and Cauchy-Schwarz Inequalities
nodes.definition: Classical algebraic inequalities relating arithmetic, geometric means and inner products, used to bound expressions and optimize under constraints.
key_facts: AM-GM: For non-negative reals a1, a2, ..., an: (a1+a2+...+an)/n >= (a1*a2*...*an)^(1/n), with equality iff all ai are equal.
Weighted AM-GM: For weights w1,...,wn summing to 1 and non-negative reals: w1*a1+...+wn*an >= a1^w1 * a2^w2 * ... * an^wn.
Cauchy-Schwarz: (a1*b1 + a2*b2 + ... + an*bn)^2 <= (a1^2+...+an^2)*(b1^2+...+bn^2), equality iff ai/bi is constant.
Engel/Titu form of Cauchy-Schwarz: a1^2/b1 + a2^2/b2 + ... + an^2/bn >= (a1+a2+...+an)^2/(b1+b2+...+bn) for positive bi.
AM-GM applied to two terms: (a+b)/2 >= sqrt(a*b) implies a+b >= 2*sqrt(a*b) for non-negative a, b.

worked_examples.problem: Given positive reals x, y, z with x + y + z = 9, find the maximum value of x^(1/3) * y^(1/3) * z^(1/3).
solution_steps: Step 1: We want to maximize P = (xyz)^(1/3) subject to x+y+z = 9.
Step 2: By AM-GM, (x+y+z)/3 >= (xyz)^(1/3).
Step 3: Substituting x+y+z = 9: 9/3 >= (xyz)^(1/3), so 3 >= (xyz)^(1/3).
Step 4: Therefore (xyz)^(1/3) <= 3, with equality when x = y = z = 3.
Step 5: Verify: x=y=z=3 gives x+y+z=9 and (3*3*3)^(1/3) = 3. Confirmed.
worked_examples.final_answer: Maximum value is 3, achieved at x = y = z = 3.
worked_examples.key_insight: AM-GM directly converts a sum constraint into a product bound; the maximum of the geometric mean occurs when all variables are equal.

worked_examples.problem: For positive reals p and q satisfying 3p + 5q = 30, find the minimum value of 1/p + 1/q.
solution_steps: Step 1: We need to minimize f = 1/p + 1/q given 3p + 5q = 30.
Step 2: Use Cauchy-Schwarz in Titu/Engel form: (1/p + 1/q) = (1^2/p + 1^2/q).
Step 3: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz: (3p+5q)(1/p + 1/q) >= (sqrt(3) + sqrt(5))^2 = 3 + 2*sqrt(15) + 5 = 8 + 2*sqrt(15).
Step 4: This uses the standard Cauchy-Schwarz: (a1^2/b1 + a2^2/b2)(b1*c1^2 + b2*c2^2) >= (a1*c1 + a2*c2)^2 form. More directly: (3p+5q)(1/p+1/q) >= (sqrt(3)+sqrt(5))^2.
Step 6: Equality holds when 3p/(1/p) = 5q/(1/q), i.e., 3p^2 = 5q^2, so p*sqrt(3) = q*sqrt(5), meaning p = q*sqrt(5/3).
Step 7: Substitute back: 3*q*sqrt(5/3) + 5q = 30, so q*(3*sqrt(5/3)+5) = 30, giving q = 30/(sqrt(45)+5) = 30/(3*sqrt(5)+5).
worked_examples.key_insight: Multiplying the constraint by the target expression and applying Cauchy-Schwarz yields the bound cleanly; equality condition determines the optimal point.

worked_examples.problem: Show that for positive reals a, b, c: a/(b+c) + b/(a+c) + c/(a+b) >= 3/2.
solution_steps: Step 1: Let S = a+b+c. Rewrite each fraction: a/(b+c) = a/(S-a).
Step 2: Note a/(S-a) = (S - (S-a))/(S-a) = S/(S-a) - 1.
Step 3: So the sum = S*(1/(b+c) + 1/(a+c) + 1/(a+b)) - 3.
Step 5: Therefore the sum >= S*(9/(2S)) - 3 = 9/2 - 3 = 3/2.
Step 6: Equality holds when b+c = a+c = a+b, i.e., a = b = c.
worked_examples.final_answer: a/(b+c) + b/(a+c) + c/(a+b) >= 3/2, with equality when a = b = c.
worked_examples.key_insight: Nesbitt's inequality is elegantly proved by rewriting fractions to isolate a sum of reciprocals, then applying Cauchy-Schwarz in Titu form to that sum.

common_pitfalls: Pitfall 1: Applying AM-GM to expressions that can be negative — AM-GM requires all terms to be non-negative; forgetting this leads to invalid inequalities.
Pitfall 2: Forgetting to verify the equality condition — just finding the bound is insufficient; you must confirm the equality case is achievable within the given constraints.
Pitfall 3: Misapplying Titu/Engel form by placing the wrong terms in numerator vs denominator — the form is sum(ai^2/bi), not sum(ai/bi^2).

nodes.title: Inradius and Circumradius Formulas
nodes.definition: In geometry, the inradius (r) is the radius of the largest circle fitting inside a polygon, while the circumradius (R) is the radius of the circle passing through all vertices.
key_facts: fact 1: For any triangle with area A, semiperimeter s, inradius r = A / s
fact 2: For any triangle with sides a, b, c and area A, circumradius R = (a * b * c) / (4 * A)
fact 3: Extended law of sines: a / sin(A) = 2R, so R = a / (2 * sin(A))
fact 4: For a right triangle with hypotenuse c, circumradius R = c / 2
fact 5: For a right triangle with legs a, b and hypotenuse c, inradius r = (a + b - c) / 2
fact 6: Euler's inequality: R >= 2r, with equality only for equilateral triangles
fact 7: For an equilateral triangle with side a: r = a / (2 * sqrt(3)), R = a / sqrt(3), and R = 2r

worked_examples.problem: A triangle has sides of length 13, 14, and 15. Find its inradius and circumradius.
solution_steps: Step 1: Compute the semiperimeter s = (13 + 14 + 15) / 2 = 21.
Step 2: Apply Heron's formula to find area A = sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)) = sqrt(21 * 8 * 7 * 6) = sqrt(7056) = 84.
Step 3: Inradius r = A / s = 84 / 21 = 4.
worked_examples.key_insight: Heron's formula bridges side lengths to area, enabling both r and R to be computed purely from side lengths. The 13-14-15 triangle is a classic integer-sided triangle with integer inradius.

worked_examples.problem: A triangle has angles 30°, 60°, 90° and its shortest side (opposite 30°) has length 7. Find its inradius and circumradius.
solution_steps: Step 1: Identify sides using the 30-60-90 ratio. Shortest side a = 7 (opposite 30°), so b = 7*sqrt(3) (opposite 60°), c = 14 (hypotenuse, opposite 90°).
Step 2: Circumradius using right-triangle rule: R = c / 2 = 14 / 2 = 7.
Step 3: Compute semiperimeter s = (7 + 7*sqrt(3) + 14) / 2 = (21 + 7*sqrt(3)) / 2.
Step 4: Compute area A = (1/2) * a * b = (1/2) * 7 * 7*sqrt(3) = 49*sqrt(3)/2.
Step 6: Simplify by factoring 7 from denominator: r = 49*sqrt(3) / (7*(3 + sqrt(3))) = 7*sqrt(3) / (3 + sqrt(3)).

Step 7: Rationalize: multiply numerator and denominator by (3 - sqrt(3)): r = 7*sqrt(3)*(3 - sqrt(3)) / ((3 + sqrt(3))(3 - sqrt(3))) = 7*(3*sqrt(3) - 3) / (9 - 3) = 7*(3*sqrt(3) - 3) / 6 = 7*(sqrt(3) - 1)*3/6 = 7*(sqrt(3) - 1)/2.
Step 8: Verify using the right-triangle formula: r = (a + b - c)/2 = (7 + 7*sqrt(3) - 14)/2 = 7*(sqrt(3) - 1)/2. Confirmed.
worked_examples.key_insight: For right triangles, R = c/2 provides an instant shortcut. The special formula r = (a + b - c)/2 for right triangles avoids computing area entirely and serves as a useful verification.

worked_examples.problem: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides of length 10 and a base of length 12. Find r and R, and verify Euler's inequality R >= 2r.
solution_steps: Step 1: Semiperimeter s = (10 + 10 + 12) / 2 = 16.
Step 2: Height from apex to base h = sqrt(10^2 - 6^2) = sqrt(64) = 8.
Step 4: Inradius r = A / s = 48 / 16 = 3.
Step 6: Check Euler's inequality: 2r = 6, and R = 6.25 >= 6. Confirmed R >= 2r with strict inequality since the triangle is not equilateral.
worked_examples.key_insight: Splitting the isosceles triangle with its axis of symmetry gives an easy height calculation. Euler's inequality R >= 2r provides a quick sanity check on computed values.

common_pitfalls: pitfall 1: Confusing semiperimeter s with full perimeter when using r = A/s; always divide the sum of sides by 2 first.
pitfall 2: Applying R = c/2 to non-right triangles; this shortcut is valid ONLY when c is the hypotenuse of a right triangle.
pitfall 3: Using r = (a + b - c)/2 for non-right triangles; this formula is exclusively for right triangles where c is the hypotenuse.

nodes.title: Integer Part and Fractional Part
nodes.definition: For any real number x, the integer part (floor) floor(x) is the greatest integer <= x, and the fractional part is {x} = x - floor(x), satisfying 0 <= {x} < 1.
key_facts: floor(x) + {x} = x for all real x, where {x} in [0, 1)
floor(x + n) = floor(x) + n for any integer n
{x + n} = {x} for any integer n (fractional part is periodic with period 1)
floor(-x) = -floor(x) - 1 when x is not an integer; floor(-x) = -floor(x) when x is an integer
floor(x) + floor(y) <= floor(x + y) <= floor(x) + floor(y) + 1
floor(x/n) = floor(floor(x)/n) for positive integer n (Hermite's identity variant)
Sum_{k=1}^{n} floor(x/k) counts lattice points under the hyperbola y = x/k

worked_examples.problem: Find the value of floor(17/3) + floor(34/3) + floor(51/3) + floor(68/3) + floor(85/3).
solution_steps: Compute each term: floor(17/3) = floor(5.666...) = 5
floor(51/3) = floor(17) = 17
worked_examples.key_insight: Each term floor(17k/3) can differ from 17k/3 by a fractional part; tracking which multiples of 3 are hit (k=3) versus missed reveals the pattern of rounding losses accumulating predictably.

worked_examples.problem: If {x} + {2x} = 1.7, find all possible values of {3x}.
solution_steps: Let {x} = f, so f in [0,1). Then {2x} = {2f} since {2x} = {2*floor(x) + 2f} = {2f}.
Case 1: f in [0, 0.5). Then {2f} = 2f, so f + 2f = 3f = 1.7, giving f = 17/30.
Check: 17/30 ≈ 0.5667, which is NOT in [0, 0.5). Contradiction, so Case 1 fails.
Check: 0.9 in [0.5, 1). Valid.
worked_examples.key_insight: The key is to split into cases based on whether {x} < 0.5 or >= 0.5, because this determines whether {2x} = 2{x} or 2{x} - 1. Only one case yields a consistent solution.

worked_examples.problem: Compute the sum S = sum_{k=1}^{99} floor(sqrt(k)).
solution_steps: floor(sqrt(k)) = m exactly when m^2 <= k < (m+1)^2, i.e., for (m+1)^2 - m^2 = 2m+1 values of k.
For m = 1: k in {1,2,3}, count = 3 values, contribution = 1*3 = 3.
For m = 2: k in {4,5,6,7,8}, count = 5 values, contribution = 2*5 = 10.
For m = 3: k in {9,...,15}, count = 7 values, contribution = 3*7 = 21.
For m = 4: k in {16,...,24}, count = 9 values, contribution = 4*9 = 36.
For m = 5: k in {25,...,35}, count = 11 values, contribution = 5*11 = 55.
For m = 6: k in {36,...,48}, count = 13 values, contribution = 6*13 = 78.
For m = 7: k in {49,...,63}, count = 15 values, contribution = 7*15 = 105.
For m = 8: k in {64,...,80}, count = 17 values, contribution = 8*17 = 136.
For m = 9: k in {81,...,99}, count = 19 values, contribution = 9*19 = 171.
worked_examples.key_insight: Group indices by the value of floor(sqrt(k)); each group m contributes m*(2m+1) terms, turning the sum into a finite sum over m from 1 to 9 with the last group truncated at k=99.

common_pitfalls: pitfall 1: Confusing floor(-2.3) = -3 (not -2); floor always rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero.
pitfall 2: Assuming {-x} = -{x}; in fact {-2.3} = 0.7, not -0.3, because {x} = x - floor(x) is always non-negative.
pitfall 3: Incorrectly applying floor(x*y) = floor(x)*floor(y); this fails in general, e.g., floor(1.5*1.5) = floor(2.25) = 2, but floor(1.5)*floor(1.5) = 1.

nodes.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions and Ranges
nodes.definition: Inverse trig functions (arcsin, arccos, arctan, etc.) reverse the standard trig mappings by restricting domains to ensure one-to-one correspondence, returning angles from given ratios.
key_facts: arcsin: domain [-1, 1], range [-pi/2, pi/2]; arccos: domain [-1, 1], range [0, pi]; arctan: domain all reals, range (-pi/2, pi/2)
Pythagorean identity extension: arcsin(x) + arccos(x) = pi/2 for all x in [-1, 1]
Derivative formulas: d/dx arcsin(x) = 1/sqrt(1-x^2), d/dx arccos(x) = -1/sqrt(1-x^2), d/dx arctan(x) = 1/(1+x^2)
Composition identity: sin(arcsin(x)) = x for x in [-1,1], but arcsin(sin(x)) = x ONLY when x in [-pi/2, pi/2]
Addition formula: arctan(a) + arctan(b) = arctan((a+b)/(1-ab)) + k*pi, where k depends on the sign of 1-ab
arctan(x) + arctan(1/x) = pi/2 for x > 0, and = -pi/2 for x < 0

worked_examples.problem: Evaluate arcsin(sin(7*pi/6)) without a calculator.
solution_steps: Recognize that 7*pi/6 is NOT in the principal range [-pi/2, pi/2] of arcsin.
Compute sin(7*pi/6): since 7*pi/6 = pi + pi/6, we have sin(7*pi/6) = -sin(pi/6) = -1/2.
Now find arcsin(-1/2), which asks: what angle in [-pi/2, pi/2] has sine equal to -1/2?
That angle is -pi/6, since sin(-pi/6) = -1/2 and -pi/6 is in [-pi/2, pi/2].
Therefore arcsin(sin(7*pi/6)) = -pi/6.
worked_examples.key_insight: arcsin(sin(x)) does NOT simply return x; it returns the equivalent angle within the restricted range [-pi/2, pi/2], requiring you to first evaluate the sine value and then find the principal-range angle.

worked_examples.problem: Simplify arctan(3) + arctan(1/4) into a single arctan expression, and verify whether an adjustment of pi is needed.
solution_steps: Apply the arctan addition formula: arctan(a) + arctan(b) = arctan((a+b)/(1-ab)) + k*pi.
Set a = 3, b = 1/4. Compute a + b = 3 + 1/4 = 13/4.
Form the argument: (13/4) / (1/4) = 13.
Check the sign of 1 - ab: it is 1/4 > 0, and both a, b > 0, so no pi adjustment is needed (k = 0).
Therefore arctan(3) + arctan(1/4) = arctan(13).
worked_examples.key_insight: When 1 - ab > 0 and both inputs are positive, the standard arctan addition formula applies directly without any pi correction; the correction is only needed when 1 - ab < 0 (i.e., ab > 1).

worked_examples.problem: Find the exact value of cos(arctan(5/12)).
solution_steps: Let theta = arctan(5/12), so tan(theta) = 5/12 and theta is in (-pi/2, pi/2).
Draw a right triangle: opposite side = 5, adjacent side = 12.
Compute the hypotenuse: sqrt(5^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(25 + 144) = sqrt(169) = 13.
Since theta is in (-pi/2, pi/2), cos(theta) > 0.
Therefore cos(arctan(5/12)) = adjacent/hypotenuse = 12/13.
worked_examples.key_insight: Evaluating trig functions of inverse trig expressions is most cleanly handled by constructing a right triangle from the given ratio, then reading off the desired side ratio directly.

common_pitfalls: Range confusion: assuming arcsin(sin(x)) = x for all x; the identity only holds when x is already in [-pi/2, pi/2], and outside that range you must reduce to the principal value.
Forgetting the pi correction in the arctan addition formula when ab > 1 (i.e., 1 - ab < 0), which shifts the result by pi and changes the quadrant of the answer.
Sign errors with arccos: since arccos has range [0, pi], cos(arccos(x)) = x always, but arccos(cos(x)) = x ONLY for x in [0, pi], not for arbitrary angles.

nodes.title: Isosceles Tetrahedron Properties and Formulas
nodes.definition: An isosceles tetrahedron is a tetrahedron where opposite edges are equal in pairs, making it inscribable in a rectangular parallelepiped (box).
key_facts: fact 1: An isosceles tetrahedron has three pairs of opposite edges with equal lengths: a, b, c where opposite edges match.

fact 2: Volume V = (sqrt(2)/3) * a * b * c / sqrt((a^2+b^2-c^2)(a^2+c^2-b^2)(b^2+c^2-a^2)) ... more directly V = (1/3) * base_area * height, but for the box with dimensions p, q, r: a^2 = q^2+r^2, b^2 = p^2+r^2, c^2 = p^2+q^2, and V_tetra = (1/3)*V_box = (1/3)*p*q*r.
fact 3: The circumscribed box has edge lengths p = sqrt((a^2+b^2+c^2)/2 - b^2) ... specifically p = sqrt((-a^2+b^2+c^2)/2), q = sqrt((a^2-b^2+c^2)/2), r = sqrt((a^2+b^2-c^2)/2).
fact 4: All four faces of an isosceles tetrahedron are congruent acute triangles (the tetrahedron is isosceles if and only if its four faces are congruent).
fact 5: The centroid, circumcenter, and incenter of an isosceles tetrahedron all coincide at the midpoint of the space diagonal of the circumscribed box.
fact 6: Circumradius R = sqrt(a^2+b^2+c^2)/2 where a, b, c are the three distinct edge lengths.

worked_examples.problem: An isosceles tetrahedron has opposite edge pairs of lengths 5, 7, and 8. Find the volume of the tetrahedron.
solution_steps: Step 1: Identify the three distinct edge-length pairs: a=5, b=7, c=8.
Step 2: Compute the dimensions of the circumscribed rectangular box using p = sqrt((-a^2+b^2+c^2)/2), q = sqrt((a^2-b^2+c^2)/2), r = sqrt((a^2+b^2-c^2)/2).
Step 6: Volume of box = p*q*r = 2*sqrt(11) * 2*sqrt(5) * sqrt(5) = 2*sqrt(11)*2*5 = 20*sqrt(11).
Step 7: Volume of isosceles tetrahedron = (1/3) * Volume of box = (20*sqrt(11))/3.
worked_examples.key_insight: The key trick is recognizing that an isosceles tetrahedron is always inscribed in a rectangular box and its volume equals exactly 1/3 of that box's volume, reducing the problem to finding box dimensions from edge pairs.

worked_examples.problem: An isosceles tetrahedron has all four faces congruent with side lengths 6, 7, and 9 on each face. Find the circumradius of the tetrahedron.
solution_steps: Step 1: For an isosceles tetrahedron, each face is a triangle with sides 6, 7, 9. The opposite edges of the tetrahedron pair up, so edge lengths are a=6, b=7, c=9.
Step 2: Use the circumradius formula R = sqrt(a^2+b^2+c^2)/2.
Step 4: R = sqrt(166)/2.

Step 5: Verify the box dimensions are real: p = sqrt((-36+49+81)/2) = sqrt(94/2) = sqrt(47), q = sqrt((36-49+81)/2) = sqrt(68/2) = sqrt(34), r = sqrt((36+49-81)/2) = sqrt(4/2) = sqrt(2). All positive, so valid.
Step 6: Therefore R = sqrt(166)/2 ≈ 6.44.
worked_examples.key_insight: The circumradius formula R = sqrt(a^2+b^2+c^2)/2 comes directly from the circumscribed box: R equals half the space diagonal of the box, which equals sqrt(p^2+q^2+r^2)/... noting that p^2+q^2+r^2 = (a^2+b^2+c^2)/2... wait, space diagonal = sqrt(p^2+q^2+r^2) = sqrt((a^2+b^2+c^2)/2), so R = sqrt((a^2+b^2+c^2)/2)/2... rechecking: p^2+q^2+r^2 = (-a^2+b^2+c^2)/2 + (a^2-b^2+c^2)/2 + (a^2+b^2-c^2)/2 = (a^2+b^2+c^2)/2, so R = sqrt(a^2+b^2+c^2)/2 only if space diagonal equals circumdiameter, confirming R = sqrt(p^2+q^2+r^2)/2 = sqrt((a^2+b^2+c^2)/2)/2.

common_pitfalls: pitfall 1: Confusing an isosceles tetrahedron with a regular tetrahedron — a regular tetrahedron has all 6 edges equal, while an isosceles tetrahedron has only 3 pairs of opposite edges equal (not necessarily all the same length).

pitfall 2: Forgetting to verify that the computed box dimensions p, q, r are all real (positive under the square root); if any expression is negative, the given edge lengths cannot form a valid isosceles tetrahedron.

pitfall 3: Incorrectly computing the circumradius as sqrt(a^2+b^2+c^2)/2 directly — the correct formula is R = sqrt((a^2+b^2+c^2)/2)/2 = sqrt(a^2+b^2+c^2)/(2*sqrt(2)), derived from half the space diagonal of the circumscribed box.

nodes.title: Law of Cosines Triangle Formula
nodes.definition: A generalization of the Pythagorean theorem relating all three sides and one angle of any triangle, used when two sides and the included angle or all three sides are known.
key_facts: fact 1: For triangle with sides a, b, c and angles A, B, C opposite to respective sides: c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab*cos(C)
fact 2: Symmetric forms: a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc*cos(A) and b^2 = a^2 + c^2 - 2ac*cos(B)
fact 3: Solving for angle: cos(C) = (a^2 + b^2 - c^2) / (2ab), useful in the SSS case
fact 4: When C = 90 degrees, cos(C) = 0 and the formula reduces to the Pythagorean theorem c^2 = a^2 + b^2
fact 5: If cos(C) < 0 (i.e., C is obtuse), then c^2 > a^2 + b^2, confirming the longest side is opposite the largest angle

worked_examples.problem: A triangle has sides a = 7, b = 11, and the included angle C = 40 degrees. Find the length of side c.
solution_steps: step 1: Identify the known values: a = 7, b = 11, C = 40 degrees.
step 2: Apply the law of cosines: c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab*cos(C).
step 3: Compute a^2 + b^2 = 49 + 121 = 170.
step 4: Compute 2ab = 2 * 7 * 11 = 154.
step 5: Compute cos(40 degrees) ≈ 0.7660.
worked_examples.key_insight: This is the SAS (side-angle-side) case. The law of cosines directly yields the unknown side without needing any other information, and the included angle determines how 'open' the triangle is.

worked_examples.problem: A triangle has sides a = 9, b = 13, c = 16. Find the measure of angle C (the angle opposite the longest side).
solution_steps: step 1: Identify the known values: a = 9, b = 13, c = 16. We want angle C.
step 2: Use the rearranged law of cosines: cos(C) = (a^2 + b^2 - c^2) / (2ab).
step 5: Compute 2ab = 2 * 9 * 13 = 234.
step 7: C = arccos(-0.02564) ≈ 91.47 degrees.
worked_examples.key_insight: This is the SSS case. A negative cosine value immediately tells us the angle is obtuse (greater than 90 degrees), which is consistent with c being the longest side. This is a situation where the law of sines would be ambiguous.

worked_examples.problem: Two ships leave port simultaneously. Ship A travels 30 km on a bearing of N 60 E, and Ship B travels 45 km due East. How far apart are the ships?
solution_steps: step 1: Translate bearings to a standard angle between the two paths. N 60 E means 60 degrees from North toward East, which is 30 degrees from the East axis.
step 2: Ship B travels due East (0 degrees from East axis). The angle between the two paths is 30 degrees.
step 3: Let a = 30 km (Ship A's distance), b = 45 km (Ship B's distance), and C = 30 degrees (angle between paths).
step 4: Apply law of cosines: c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab*cos(C).
step 6: cos(30 degrees) = sqrt(3)/2 ≈ 0.8660.
worked_examples.final_answer: The ships are approximately 24.22 km apart.
worked_examples.key_insight: Real-world navigation problems require careful conversion of bearings into a usable included angle before applying the formula. The key step is correctly identifying the angle between the two direction vectors.

common_pitfalls: pitfall 1: In the SSS case, computing cos(C) = (c^2 - a^2 - b^2) / (2ab) with the wrong sign — the correct formula has (a^2 + b^2 - c^2) in the numerator, not (c^2 - a^2 - b^2) which gives the negative.
pitfall 2: Forgetting to take the square root at the end; c^2 is computed correctly but the student reports c^2 as the final answer for side length c.

pitfall 3: Using the law of cosines when the law of sines would suffice (AAS or ASA case), leading to unnecessary complexity, or conversely using the law of sines in the SSS case where it creates an ambiguous-angle problem.

nodes.title: Law of Sines Triangle Ratio
nodes.definition: In any triangle, the ratio of each side length to the sine of its opposite angle is constant, equal to the diameter of the circumscribed circle.
key_facts: Formula: a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C) = 2R, where R is the circumradius
Equivalent form: sin(A)/a = sin(B)/b = sin(C)/c
Area formula derived from law of sines: Area = (a*b*sin(C))/2 = (a*b*c)/(4R)
Ambiguous case (SSA): when given two sides and a non-included angle, there may be 0, 1, or 2 valid triangles depending on whether h = b*sin(A) is less than, equal to, or greater than the given side
The law of sines applies to ALL triangles (acute, right, and obtuse), not just acute triangles

worked_examples.problem: In triangle PQR, angle P = 47°, angle Q = 73°, and side p = 14.3 (opposite to P). Find side q (opposite to Q) and the circumradius R.
solution_steps: Step 1: Find angle R = 180° - 47° - 73° = 60°
Step 2: Apply law of sines: p/sin(P) = q/sin(Q), so 14.3/sin(47°) = q/sin(73°)
Step 3: Compute sin(47°) ≈ 0.7314 and sin(73°) ≈ 0.9563
Step 5: Find circumradius using 2R = p/sin(P) = 14.3/0.7314 ≈ 19.55
worked_examples.key_insight: The common ratio a/sin(A) directly gives 2R, so the circumradius can be extracted from any known side-angle pair without extra computation.

worked_examples.problem: In triangle ABC, side a = 9, side b = 13, and angle A = 38°. Determine how many valid triangles exist and find all possible values of angle B.
solution_steps: Step 1: Use law of sines to find sin(B): sin(B)/b = sin(A)/a, so sin(B) = 13*sin(38°)/9
Step 3: Check if sin(B) <= 1: 0.8894 < 1, so at least one triangle exists
Step 4: Check the ambiguous case: since b > a (13 > 9) and angle A is acute, we must check if both solutions are valid
Step 5: First solution: B1 = arcsin(0.8894) ≈ 62.9°. Check: A + B1 = 38° + 62.9° = 100.9° < 180°, valid.
Step 6: Second solution: B2 = 180° - 62.9° = 117.1°. Check: A + B2 = 38° + 117.1° = 155.1° < 180°, also valid.
Step 7: Two triangles exist with B ≈ 62.9° or B ≈ 117.1°
worked_examples.final_answer: Two valid triangles: B ≈ 62.9° or B ≈ 117.1°
worked_examples.key_insight: The ambiguous SSA case arises when the given angle is acute and the side opposite it is shorter than the other given side; always test both arcsin solutions against the triangle angle-sum constraint.

worked_examples.problem: Triangle DEF has angle D = 112°, angle E = 31°, and the side opposite E has length 7.6. Find the area of the triangle.
solution_steps: Step 1: Find angle F = 180° - 112° - 31° = 37°
Step 2: Label sides: e = 7.6 (opposite E = 31°). Find side d (opposite D = 112°) using law of sines.
worked_examples.key_insight: After finding all sides via the law of sines, the area formula (1/2)*a*b*sin(C) can be applied using any two sides and their included angle, making area computation straightforward for AAS-given triangles.

common_pitfalls: Ambiguous case neglect: when solving SSA triangles, students often accept only the acute arcsin solution and miss the obtuse angle solution B2 = 180° - B1, potentially discarding a valid second triangle.
Ratio inversion: writing sin(A)/a = sin(B)/b is equivalent to a/sin(A) = b/sin(B), but mixing the two forms mid-calculation (e.g., a/sin(A) = sin(B)/b) produces incorrect results.

Applying law of sines to find a side when the law of cosines is needed: if the given information is SAS (two sides and included angle), the law of sines cannot be applied directly and the law of cosines must be used first.

nodes.title: Law of Total Probability
nodes.definition: Expresses the probability of an event by conditioning on a partition of the sample space, summing weighted conditional probabilities over all partition elements.
key_facts: If B_1, B_2, ..., B_n form a partition of sample space S (mutually exclusive, exhaustive), then P(A) = sum_{i=1}^{n} P(A | B_i) * P(B_i)
Two-case form: P(A) = P(A | B) * P(B) + P(A | B^c) * P(B^c), where B^c is the complement of B
Continuous analog: P(A) = integral of P(A | X=x) * f_X(x) dx over all x, for continuous random variable X
Combining with Bayes: P(B_j | A) = [P(A | B_j) * P(B_j)] / [sum_{i=1}^{n} P(A | B_i) * P(B_i)], linking total probability to posterior computation
The partition must satisfy: P(B_i intersect B_j) = 0 for i != j, and P(union of all B_i) = 1, and P(B_i) > 0 for all i

worked_examples.problem: A factory has three machines M1, M2, M3 producing 20%, 35%, and 45% of total output respectively. Defect rates are 4%, 2%, and 3%. A randomly selected item is found defective. What is the probability it was produced by M2? First, find P(defective).
